notes.title: 1. About Spanish
notes.content:
• Spanish (el español or el castellano) is spoken in Spain, Mexico, most of Central and South America,
and parts of the USA, Africa and the Caribbean.
• It is a Romance language, descended from Latin, so many words look like English words (hotel,
importante, restaurante, animal).
• Spanish is mostly phonetic: words are pronounced the way they are written, with very few exceptions.
• Questions and exclamations start with an upside-down mark: ¿Cómo estás? ¡Hola!
• Every noun is either masculine or feminine. Words like “the”, “a” and adjectives change to match.
• Verbs change their ending depending on who does the action, so the subject pronoun is often left out:
Hablo español = (I) speak Spanish.
• Sentence order is mostly the same as English: subject + verb + rest (Como pan = I eat bread).
• Spanish varies by region: Spain uses vosotros for “you all”; Latin America uses ustedes. Some
pronunciations also differ (see section 2).

notes.title: 2. Alphabet and sounds
notes.content:
Approximate English-style pronunciations are shown in the “Sounds like” column.
The alphabet (el alfabeto)
[TABLE]
Letter | Name | Letter | Name | Letter | Name
A | ah | J | HOH-tah | S | EH-seh
B | beh | K | kah | T | teh
C | seh | L | EH-leh | U | oo
D | deh | M | EH-meh | V | OO-beh (or beh KOR-tah)
E | eh | N | EH-neh | W | OO-beh DOH-bleh
F | EH-feh | Ñ | EH-nyeh | X | EH-kees
G | heh | O | oh | Y | ee-GREE-eh-gah
H | AH-cheh | P | peh | Z | SEH-tah
I | ee | Q | koo |  | 
 |  | R | EH-rreh (rolled) |  | 
[/TABLE]
Spanish has 27 letters (the English 26 plus ñ). ch and ll are written as two letters but make their own
sounds.
Special marks (los acentos y signos)
[TABLE]
Mark | Name | Example | What it does
á é í ó ú | tilde / acento | café, está | Shows which syllable is stressed. Does not change the vowel sound
ñ | eñe | español, año (year) | Sounds like “ny” in “canyon”
ü | diéresis | pingüino (penguin) | Pronounce the u: “gwee” instead of “gee”
¿ ? | question marks | ¿Dónde estás? | Open and close every question
¡ ! | exclamation marks | ¡Qué bien! | Open and close every exclamation
[/TABLE]
Accents change meaning: si (if) vs sí (yes); tu (your) vs tú (you); el (the) vs él (he); solo (alone) vs sólo
(only, old spelling).
Vowel sounds
Spanish has only five vowel sounds. They are short, clear and never change.
[TABLE]
Vowel | Sounds like | Example
a | “ah” as in “father” | casa (house) KAH-sah
e | “eh” as in “bed” | mesa (table) MEH-sah
i | “ee” as in “see” | sí see
o | “oh” as in “go” (shorter) | oro (gold) OH-roh
u | “oo” as in “food” | uno OO-noh
ai, ay | “eye” | aire (air)
au | “ow” as in “cow” | auto (car)
ei, ey | “ay” as in “day” | rey (king)
ia, ie, io | “yah”, “yeh”, “yoh” | bien (well) byen
ua, ue, ui | “wah”, “weh”, “wee” | bueno (good) BWEH-noh
[/TABLE]
Consonant sounds
[TABLE]
Spelling | Sounds like | Example
b, v | Both sound like “b” (softer between vowels) | vaca (cow) BAH-kah; bebé
c before a, o, u | “k” | casa, cosa
c before e, i | “s” in Latin America; “th” as in “think” in most of Spain | cine (cinema) SEE-neh
z | “s” in Latin America; “th” in most of Spain | zapato (shoe)
ch | “ch” as in “chair” | chocolate
g before a, o, u | hard “g” as in “go” | gato (cat)
g before e, i | harsh “h” (from the throat) | gente (people) HEN-teh
gu before e, i | hard “g”; the u is silent | guerra (war), guitarra
j | harsh “h” | jamón (ham) hah-MOHN
h | always silent | hola OH-lah, hotel oh-TEL
ll | “y” as in “yes” (most regions) | llamo YAH-moh
y | “y” as in “yes”; alone it means “and” and sounds like “ee” | yo (I), tú y yo
ñ | “ny” | mañana mah-NYAH-nah
qu | “k”; the u is silent | queso (cheese) KEH-soh
r | a quick tap of the tongue, like “tt” in American “butter” | pero (but)
rr, or r at the start of a word | rolled (trilled) r | perro (dog), rojo (red)
d | “d”; between vowels, soft like “th” in “this” | dedo (finger)
x | “ks” | taxi; (exception: México uses the harsh “h”)
[/TABLE]
Where to stress a word
• Words ending in a vowel, n or s are stressed on the second-to-last syllable: CA-sa, HA-blas, HA-blan,
LI-bro.
• Words ending in any other consonant are stressed on the last syllable: ha-BLAR, ciu-DAD, ma-DRID.
• A written accent mark overrides these rules and shows the stress: ca-FÉ, can-CIÓN, Mé-xi-co.
• Pronounce every letter except h and the u in qu and gue/gui.

notes.title: 3. Greetings and politeness
notes.content:
[TABLE]
Spanish | Sounds like | Meaning
Hola | OH-lah | Hello / Hi
Buenos días | BWEH-nohs DEE-ahs | Good morning
Buenas tardes | BWEH-nahs TAR-dehs | Good afternoon (until about dark)
Buenas noches | BWEH-nahs NOH-chehs | Good evening / Good night
Adiós | ah-DYOHS | Goodbye
Hasta luego | AH-stah LWEH-goh | See you later
Hasta mañana | AH-stah mah-NYAH-nah | See you tomorrow
Hasta pronto | AH-stah PROHN-toh | See you soon
Gracias | GRAH-syahs | Thank you
Muchas gracias | MOO-chahs GRAH-syahs | Thank you very much
De nada | deh NAH-dah | You’re welcome (literally “of nothing”)
Por favor | pohr fah-BOHR | Please
Perdón | pehr-DOHN | Excuse me / Sorry
Disculpe | dees-KOOL-peh | Excuse me (formal, to get attention)
Lo siento | loh SYEN-toh | I’m sorry
Sí / No | see / noh | Yes / No
Vale / De acuerdo | BAH-leh / deh ah-KWEHR-doh | OK / Agreed (vale is common in Spain)
¿Cómo estás? | KOH-moh eh-STAHS | How are you? (informal)
¿Cómo está usted? | KOH-moh eh-STAH oos-TEHD | How are you? (formal)
¿Qué tal? | keh tahl | How’s it going? (informal)
Estoy bien | eh-STOY byen | I’m fine
Más o menos | mahs oh MEH-nohs | So-so
Mucho gusto | MOO-choh GOOS-toh | Nice to meet you
¿Y tú? / ¿Y usted? | ee too / ee oos-TEHD | And you? (informal / formal)
Bienvenido(a) | byen-beh-NEE-doh | Welcome
[/TABLE]
Tú or usted? Tú is for one friend, family member or child. Usted is for one person you do not know well,
someone older or in authority. In some regions people use vos instead of tú, but tú is understood everywhere.

notes.title: 4. Introducing yourself
notes.content:
[TABLE]
Spanish | Meaning
Me llamo Manu. | My name is Manu.
¿Cómo te llamas? | What is your name? (informal)
¿Cómo se llama usted? | What is your name? (formal)
Mucho gusto. / Encantado(a). | Nice to meet you. (add -a if you are female)
Soy indio / india. | I am Indian (male / female).
Soy de la India. | I am from India.
¿De dónde eres? | Where are you from? (informal)
Vivo en la India. | I live in India.
Tengo treinta años. | I am thirty years old (literally “I have thirty years”).
Soy estudiante. | I am a student.
Trabajo en una oficina. | I work in an office.
Hablo hindi y un poco de español. | I speak Hindi and a little Spanish.
No entiendo. | I don’t understand.
Hable más despacio, por favor. | Please speak more slowly.
¿Cómo se dice … en español? | How do you say … in Spanish?
[/TABLE]
Word-by-word breakdown
Me llamo Manu.
[TABLE]
Me myself | llamo (I) call | Manu Manu
[/TABLE]
Literal meaning: “I call myself Manu.” This is how Spanish says “My name is Manu.”
Vivo en Ajmer.
[TABLE]
Vivo (I) live | en in | Ajmer Ajmer
[/TABLE]
There is no word for “I”: the ending -o on vivo already means “I”.
Soy estudiante y me gusta el español.
[TABLE]
Soy (I) am | estudiante student | y and | me to me | gusta is pleasing | el the
español Spanish |  |  |  |  | 
[/TABLE]
Literal meaning: “I am a student and the Spanish is pleasing to me.” This is how Spanish says “I like
Spanish.”
Sample conversation
A: ¡Hola! ¿Cómo se llama usted?
Hello! What is your name?
B: Me llamo Priya. ¿Y usted?
My name is Priya. And you?
A: Me llamo Marcos. ¡Mucho gusto!
My name is Marcos. Nice to meet you!
B: Encantada. ¿Cómo está?
Nice to meet you. How are you?
A: Estoy bien, gracias. ¡Hasta luego!
I’m well, thank you. See you later!

notes.title: 5. Subject pronouns
notes.content:
A subject pronoun tells you who does the action. In Spanish you can usually leave it out, because the verb
ending already shows who.
[TABLE]
Spanish | Meaning | Notes
yo | I | Not capitalised unless it starts a sentence
tú | you (one person) | Informal
él | he | 
ella | she | 
usted (Ud.) | you (one person, formal) | Uses the same verb form as él / ella
nosotros / nosotras | we (masculine or mixed / all feminine) | 
vosotros / vosotras | you all (informal) | Used mainly in Spain
ellos / ellas | they (masculine or mixed / all feminine) | 
ustedes (Uds.) | you all (formal in Spain; the normal “you all” in Latin America) | Uses the same verb form as ellos / ellas
[/TABLE]
• Use the pronoun for emphasis or clarity: Yo soy Manu, ¿y tú?
• “It” is usually not translated: Es grande. = It is big.
• Reflexive pronouns used with some verbs: me, te, se, nos, os, se (me llamo = I call myself).

notes.title: 6. Nouns and articles
notes.content:
Gender
• Every noun is masculine (masculino) or feminine (femenino), including objects: el libro (the book, m.),
la mesa (the table, f.).
• Most nouns ending in -o are masculine; most ending in -a are feminine: el niño / la niña (boy / girl).
• Feminine endings: -ción, -sión, -dad, -tad, -umbre (la nación, la ciudad).
• Masculine endings: -aje, -or, -ambre (el viaje, el amor).
• Common exceptions: el día (day), el mapa (map), el problema (problem), el idioma (language) are
masculine; la mano (hand), la foto (photo) are feminine.
• Always learn a noun together with its article.
Articles
[TABLE]
Type | Masc. singular | Fem. singular | Masc. plural | Fem. plural
Definite (the) | el | la | los | las
Indefinite (a / an / some) | un | una | unos | unas
[/TABLE]
• el chico (the boy), la chica (the girl), los libros (the books), las casas (the houses)
• un libro (a book), una casa (a house), unos amigos (some friends)
• Spanish has no separate word for “some” with uncountable things: Bebo agua. = I drink (some) water.
Como pan. = I eat (some) bread.
• Feminine nouns starting with a stressed a take el in the singular: el agua (the water), but las aguas.
• Use the definite article with general ideas: Me gusta la música. = I like music.
• Do not use an article with professions after ser: Es médico. = He is a doctor.
Plurals
• Nouns ending in a vowel add -s: libro → libros, casa → casas.
• Nouns ending in a consonant add -es: ciudad → ciudades, papel → papeles.
• Nouns ending in -z change to -ces: lápiz → lápices.
• Nouns ending in an unstressed -s stay the same: el lunes → los lunes.
• Accents may be added or dropped to keep the stress: canción → canciones, joven → jóvenes.
• A mixed group of males and females uses the masculine plural: los hermanos = brothers, or brothers
and sisters.

notes.title: 7. Three key verbs: ser, estar, tener
notes.content:
Spanish has two verbs meaning “to be”: ser and estar.
[TABLE]
Pronoun | ser (to be) | estar (to be) | tener (to have)
yo | soy | estoy | tengo
tú | eres | estás | tienes
él / ella / usted | es | está | tiene
nosotros / nosotras | somos | estamos | tenemos
vosotros / vosotras | sois | estáis | tenéis
ellos / ellas / ustedes | son | están | tienen
[/TABLE]
Using ser (permanent qualities)
• Identity and description: Soy Manu. Ella es alta. (She is tall.)
• Profession, nationality and origin: Es médico. Somos de la India.
• Time and date: Es lunes. Son las tres.
• What something is made of or who owns it: Es de madera. (It’s made of wood.)
Using estar (states and locations)
• Location: Madrid está en España. Estoy en casa.
• Temporary condition or feeling: Estoy cansado. (I’m tired.) Está enfermo. (He is sick.)
• Actions in progress: Estoy estudiando. (I am studying.)
Compare: Es aburrido = he is boring (his character). Está aburrido = he is bored (right now).
Using tener
• Possession: Tengo un hermano. (I have a brother.)
• Age: ¿Cuántos años tienes? (How old are you?) Tengo diez años.
• Feelings with tener: tengo hambre (I’m hungry), sed (thirsty), frío (cold), calor (hot), miedo (afraid),
sueño (sleepy), prisa (in a hurry).
• tener que + infinitive = have to: Tengo que estudiar.
• Hay = there is / there are (from haber, never changes): Hay un gato. Hay dos gatos.

notes.title: 8. Regular verbs and common irregular verbs
notes.content:
The three verb groups
• Every verb in its dictionary form (the infinitive) ends in -ar, -er or -ir. Remove those two letters, then add
the endings below.
[TABLE]
Pronoun | -ar: hablar (to speak) | -er: comer (to eat) | -ir: vivir (to live)
yo | hablo | como | vivo
tú | hablas | comes | vives
él / ella / usted | habla | come | vive
nosotros | hablamos | comemos | vivimos
vosotros | habláis | coméis | vivís
ellos / ustedes | hablan | comen | viven
[/TABLE]
[TABLE]
Verb | Meaning | Verb | Meaning
hablar | to speak | comer | to eat
trabajar | to work | beber | to drink
estudiar | to study | leer | to read
escuchar | to listen | aprender | to learn
mirar | to look at / watch | vender | to sell
cantar | to sing | vivir | to live
bailar | to dance | escribir | to write
comprar | to buy | abrir | to open
[/TABLE]
• Spanish has one present tense for both “I speak” and “I am speaking”: Hablo.
• The verb ending already shows the person, so hablamos alone means “we speak”.
Very common irregular verbs
[TABLE]
Pronoun | ir (to go) | hacer (to do / make) | poder (can) | querer (to want)
yo | voy | hago | puedo | quiero
tú | vas | haces | puedes | quieres
él / ella / usted | va | hace | puede | quiere
nosotros | vamos | hacemos | podemos | queremos
vosotros | vais | hacéis | podéis | queréis
ellos / ustedes | van | hacen | pueden | quieren
[/TABLE]
• Voy a la escuela. = I go to school.
• Voy a comer. = I am going to eat (ir a + infinitive = near future).
• Quiero un café. = I want a coffee. Quisiera un café. = I would like a coffee (more polite).
• Hace calor. = It is hot (weather uses hacer).
• Puedo + infinitive = I can: Puedo ayudar.
• Stem-changing verbs (poder, querer) change the vowel in the stem for yo, tú, él, ellos but not for
nosotros and vosotros: o→ue (puedo), e→ie (quiero).

notes.title: 9. Saying “not”
notes.content:
• Put no directly before the verb: Hablo inglés → No hablo inglés (I don’t speak English).
• There is no helper word like English “do”: No como carne. = I don’t eat meat.
• Short answers: ¿Tienes hambre? — No, no tengo hambre.
• Spanish uses double negatives, and they are correct: No tengo nada. = I have nothing (literally “I
don’t have nothing”).
[TABLE]
Spanish | Meaning | Example
no | no / not | No está aquí. (He is not here.)
nunca | never | Nunca como carne. / No como carne nunca.
nada | nothing | No entiendo nada.
nadie | nobody | No conozco a nadie.
tampoco | neither / not either | Yo tampoco. (Me neither.)
ya no | no longer | Ya no vive aquí.
[/TABLE]

notes.title: 10. Asking questions
notes.content:
Ways to ask a yes/no question
• Raise your voice and write ¿ ?: ¿Hablas español? (most common)
• Put the subject after the verb: ¿Habla Ana español?
• Add ¿verdad? or ¿no? at the end for “right?”: Eres estudiante, ¿verdad?
Question words (always written with an accent)
[TABLE]
Spanish | Meaning | Example
qué | what | ¿Qué es esto? (What is this?)
quién / quiénes | who | ¿Quién es ella?
dónde | where | ¿Dónde vives?
cuándo | when | ¿Cuándo llegas?
por qué | why | ¿Por qué estudias español?
porque | because (answer, one word, no accent) | Porque me gusta.
cómo | how | ¿Cómo estás?
cuánto / cuánta | how much | ¿Cuánto cuesta? (How much does it cost?)
cuántos / cuántas | how many | ¿Cuántos años tienes?
cuál / cuáles | which | ¿Cuál prefieres?
[/TABLE]
¿Qué hora es? = What time is it? Esto es = this is. Eso es = that is.

notes.title: 11. Numbers
notes.content:
[TABLE]
No. | Spanish | No. | Spanish | No. | Spanish
0 | cero | 7 | siete | 14 | catorce
1 | uno / una | 8 | ocho | 15 | quince
2 | dos | 9 | nueve | 16 | dieciséis
3 | tres | 10 | diez | 17 | diecisiete
4 | cuatro | 11 | once | 18 | dieciocho
5 | cinco | 12 | doce | 19 | diecinueve
6 | seis | 13 | trece | 20 | veinte
[/TABLE]
Tens and above
[TABLE]
No. | Spanish | No. | Spanish
20 | veinte | 60 | sesenta
30 | treinta | 70 | setenta
40 | cuarenta | 80 | ochenta
50 | cincuenta | 90 | noventa
[/TABLE]
• 21 to 29 are one word: veintiuno (21), veintidós (22), veintitrés (23).
• From 31, use y (and) between tens and units: treinta y uno (31), cuarenta y cinco (45), noventa y
nueve (99).
• 100 = cien (exactly 100) or ciento before more: ciento uno (101).
• 200 = doscientos, 300 = trescientos, 500 = quinientos, 700 = setecientos, 900 = novecientos.
• 1000 = mil, 2000 = dos mil, 1,000,000 = un millón.
• uno becomes un before a masculine noun and una before a feminine noun: un libro, veintiuna casas.
Ordinal numbers
primero (1st), segundo (2nd), tercero (3rd), cuarto (4th), quinto (5th). They agree in gender: la primera
vez (the first time). Primero and tercero shorten to primer and tercer before a masculine noun.

notes.title: 12. Days, months, seasons and time
notes.content:
[TABLE]
Day | Meaning | Month | Meaning
lunes | Monday | enero | January
martes | Tuesday | febrero | February
miércoles | Wednesday | marzo | March
jueves | Thursday | abril | April
viernes | Friday | mayo | May
sábado | Saturday | junio | June
domingo | Sunday | julio | July
 |  | agosto | August
[/TABLE]
[TABLE]
Day | Meaning | Month | Meaning
 |  | septiembre | September
 |  | octubre | October
 |  | noviembre | November
 |  | diciembre | December
[/TABLE]
• Days and months are not capitalised in Spanish. The week starts on Monday.
• Date format is day first, with de: el 17 de octubre. The first of the month can be el primero de mayo
or el uno de mayo.
• “On Monday” = el lunes; “on Mondays” = los lunes.
• Seasons: la primavera (spring), el verano (summer), el otoño (autumn), el invierno (winter).
Telling time and time words
• ¿Qué hora es? = What time is it?
• One o’clock uses singular: Es la una. Other hours use plural: Son las tres. (It is three o’clock.)
• Es mediodía = noon. Es medianoche = midnight.
• y cuarto = quarter past; y media = half past; menos cuarto = quarter to: Son las tres y media.
(3:30)
• hoy (today), mañana (tomorrow; also “morning”), ayer (yesterday), ahora (now), la mañana
(morning), la tarde (afternoon), la noche (night).
• la semana (week), el mes (month), el año (year), el día (day).

notes.title: 13. Everyday words
notes.content:
Family (la familia)
[TABLE]
Spanish | Meaning | Spanish | Meaning
el padre / el papá | father / dad | la madre / la mamá | mother / mom
el hermano | brother | la hermana | sister
el hijo | son | la hija | daughter
el abuelo | grandfather | la abuela | grandmother
el tío | uncle | la tía | aunt
el esposo / el marido | husband | la esposa / la mujer | wife (mujer also means woman)
el amigo / la amiga | friend (m. / f.) | el niño / la niña | boy / girl, child
[/TABLE]
Colours (los colores)
[TABLE]
Spanish | Meaning | Spanish | Meaning
rojo(a) | red | azul | blue
verde | green | amarillo(a) | yellow
negro(a) | black | blanco(a) | white
gris | grey | naranja | orange
rosa | pink | marrón | brown
[/TABLE]
Food and drink (la comida)
[TABLE]
Spanish | Meaning | Spanish | Meaning
el agua (f.) | water | el pan | bread
la leche | milk | el queso | cheese
el café | coffee | el arroz | rice
el té | tea | la carne | meat
el jugo / el zumo | juice (Latin America / Spain) | el pescado | fish
la manzana | apple | el huevo | egg
el plátano | banana | la verdura | vegetable
el desayuno | breakfast | el almuerzo / la cena | lunch / dinner
[/TABLE]
Places and things
[TABLE]
Spanish | Meaning | Spanish | Meaning
la casa | house / home | la escuela | school
la ciudad | city | la oficina | office
la calle | street | la tienda | shop
la estación | station | el hospital | hospital
el libro | book | el bolígrafo | pen
el coche / el carro | car | el teléfono | phone
el dinero | money | el trabajo | work / job
[/TABLE]
Body and feelings
la cabeza (head), la mano (hand), el pie (foot), la cara (face), el ojo / los ojos (eye / eyes). Feelings with
estar: contento(a) (happy), triste (sad), cansado(a) (tired), enfermo(a) (sick).

notes.title: 14. Adjectives, possessives and “this/that”
notes.content:
Adjective agreement
• Adjectives match the noun in gender and number.
• Adjectives ending in -o change to -a for feminine: alto → alta, pequeño → pequeña.
• Adjectives ending in -e or most consonants have the same form for both genders: grande, inteligente,
fácil, azul.
• Plural: add -s after a vowel, -es after a consonant: altos, altas, fáciles.
• Nationalities ending in a consonant add -a for feminine: español → española.
• Most adjectives go after the noun: un coche rojo (a red car).
• bueno, malo, grande shorten before a masculine singular noun: un buen amigo, un mal día, un gran
libro.
[TABLE]
Masculine | Feminine | Meaning
alto | alta | tall / high
bajo | baja | short / low
[/TABLE]
[TABLE]
Masculine | Feminine | Meaning
bueno | buena | good
malo | mala | bad
nuevo | nueva | new
viejo | vieja | old
bonito | bonita | pretty / nice
grande | grande | big
pequeño | pequeña | small
fácil | fácil | easy
difícil | difícil | difficult
feliz | feliz | happy
[/TABLE]
Possessive adjectives (my, your, his…)
[TABLE]
Meaning | Singular noun | Plural noun
my | mi | mis
your (tú) | tu | tus
his / her / your (usted) / their | su | sus
our | nuestro / nuestra | nuestros / nuestras
your (vosotros) | vuestro / vuestra | vuestros / vuestras
[/TABLE]
• The form depends on the thing owned (singular or plural), not on the owner: mi hermano (my brother),
mis hermanos (my brothers).
• su can mean his, her, your (formal) or their. Context tells you which.
Demonstratives (this, that)
[TABLE]
Meaning | Masc. | Fem. | Masc. pl. | Fem. pl.
this / these (near) | este | esta | estos | estas
that / those (a bit far) | ese | esa | esos | esas
that / those (far away) | aquel | aquella | aquellos | aquellas
[/TABLE]
este libro (this book), esa casa (that house), estos niños (these children).

notes.title: 15. Small words you need
notes.content:
[TABLE]
Spanish | Meaning | Spanish | Meaning
y (e before “i”) | and | o (u before “o”) | or
pero | but | entonces | so / then

Contractions with a and de
• a + el = al: Voy al mercado. (I go to the market.)
• de + el = del: el libro del profesor (the teacher’s book).
• a la, a los, a las, de la, de los, de las do not contract.
• Personal a: put a before a person who receives the action: Veo a María. (I see María.) but Veo la casa.
Liking things with gustar
• gustar means “to be pleasing”. The thing liked is the subject, so the verb matches it.
• One thing: Me gusta el café. (I like coffee.) Several things: Me gustan los libros. (I like books.)
• Who likes it: me (I), te (you), le (he / she / you formal), nos (we), les (they / you all).
• With a verb, always use gusta: Me gusta bailar. (I like dancing.)
• Negative: No me gusta la leche. (I don’t like milk.)
Useful survival phrases
• Quisiera … = I would like …
• ¿Dónde está la estación? = Where is the station?
• ¿Cuánto cuesta? = How much does it cost?
• La cuenta, por favor. = The bill, please.
• No sé. = I don’t know.
• ¿Puede ayudarme? = Can you help me?
• ¿Habla inglés? = Do you speak English?
• Repita, por favor. = Please repeat.
